The screening room fell dark as the newsreel obituary recapped Emmett Rusk’s public life, ending with his death alone at Silvermount and closing without explaining his enigmatic last word. The editor turned to the reporter Nash, assigning him to discover what "Bluebell" meant. Nash’s quest began at a seaside nightclub, where a drunk Nora turned him away at the door without answers.

Determined, Nash sat in a quiet archive opening the bound memoir of the late banker Barrow, slipping back into the past. 

Years ago, in a dusty western mining boarding house, Emmett’s mother had signed her young son over to Barrow after a defaulted lodger’s mine deed suddenly made the family rich. Infuriated by the trade, the boy had driven his sled directly into Barrow’s stomach, but he was dragged away east from his parents anyway. On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett formally took control of the immense fortune and informed Barrow that out of all his vast holdings, he wanted only to run a failing city newspaper, the Clarion.

Nash closed the memoir and sought out Marsh, Rusk’s long-serving manager, to hear how the empire was built. 

Marsh recalled the triumphant early days when Emmett moved directly into the Clarion, installed Marsh alongside his childhood friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Soon after, Emmett boldly hired away the entire staff of their rival paper and celebrated with a grand party featuring a loud brass band and a line of chorus girls.

Next, Nash tracked down Devlin in his quiet exile to piece together the middle years. 

Devlin recounted how Emmett had returned from a lavish buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor’s niece. But love faded quickly; a famous run of quiet breakfast-table scenes charted their marriage cooling into total silence behind separate raised newspapers. Then came the scandal. Emmett met a modest shopgirl, Nora Kell, on the street after getting mud on his coat, and soon began visiting her private rooms in secret. Mid-campaign during Emmett’s run for governor, the ruthless party boss Halloran brought Adele straight to Nora’s apartment, threatening exposure unless Emmett withdrew. Emmett stubbornly refused. He lost the election, a disillusioned Devlin asked to be transferred to another city, and Emmett's first marriage collapsed completely.

Nash then managed a brief audience with Nora herself. She spoke bitterly of what followed. 

After the divorce, Emmett married Nora and forced her into a grand opera career for which she possessed no actual voice. Her disastrous debut was a public humiliation. A drunk Devlin began writing a savage review for the Clarion, but Emmett finished the scathing critique himself, printed it, and promptly fired Devlin. Nora, driven to despair, swallowed poison rather than sing again, and only then did Emmett finally let her stop performing. He shut her away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she spent years working endless jigsaw puzzles in the vast, echoing hall. Finally, after a joyless beach picnic and a heated quarrel, Nora packed her bags and left him forever. 

Lastly, Nash interviewed the aging butler, Colm, regarding Rusk’s final hours. 

Colm remembered the afternoon Nora left. Enraged, Emmett had wrecked her empty bedroom, discovered a heavy glass snow globe, murmured "Bluebell," and carried it past the endless hall of mirrors. Years later, isolated and alone at Silvermount, Emmett died with that same word on his lips, dropping the glass snow globe to shatter on the marble floor.

Having read Barrow’s memoir and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and Colm, Nash stood in the cavernous, cluttered hall of Silvermount as liquidation men tagged the dead tycoon’s endless possessions. Nash sighed, concluding to his fellow journalists that no single word could ever explain a man's life. Deep in the basement below them, oblivious to the secret, workmen shoveled a mountain of discarded junk into the roaring furnace, including a faded wooden child’s sled plainly marked *Bluebell*.

Mr. Ash cradled the screaming, blood-soaked Mr. Elm on the concrete floor of the abandoned warehouse, swearing fiercely that he was not going to die. Moments later, Mr. Birch arrived, shouting that the robbery had been a setup orchestrated by an insider, before hurrying outside to hide the stashed diamonds. Before the tension could ease, Mr. Cedar strolled into the room, grinning as he dragged a bound patrolman named Doyle from the boot of his car.

It felt a world away from the diner earlier that week, right after Ren Vasco had walked out of prison to report to Bram and Cal, who owed him for years of silent loyalty. Over breakfast, the crew had loudly argued over the true meaning of a pop song and whether waitresses deserved a tip. That was when Bram had handed out the tree aliases, ignoring Mr. Birch when he vehemently objected to his assigned name.

Back in the warehouse, Cedar left the others and turned on a radio oldie. He began to dance, laughing as he sliced off Doyle’s ear and doused the squirming officer in petrol. From his prone position on the floor, Elm summoned his last strength, raised his gun, and shot Cedar dead. Elm dragged himself toward the bleeding officer, whispering that he was an undercover cop and that the police were already surrounding the building waiting for Bram. But when Cal returned, he listened coolly to Elm’s frantic account of Cedar’s madness, stepped forward, and executed Doyle with a single bullet.

In the agonizing wait, Elm’s mind drifted back to the handler who had made him. Undercover officer Danny Roarke had rehearsed a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet with Pruitt, practicing until he could tell it as if it were his own cherished memory. He had performed the story perfectly for Bram, Cal, and Mr. Ash, earning his place on the crew as Mr. Elm. Then the heist had collapsed within a minute. Ash had shot his way clear of the police from the getaway car with Elm beside him, but fleeing on foot afterward, Elm had hijacked a car and been shot in the stomach by its terrified driver, whom Elm had shot dead in response.

The warehouse door slammed open as Bram arrived, instantly declaring Mr. Elm to be the police informer. Ash refused to believe the boss, raising his own weapon and pointing it directly at Bram to defend his dying friend. The resulting three-way standoff erupted into gunfire, leaving Bram, Cal, and Ash all hit and bleeding on the dust-choked floor, with only Ash and Elm still breathing. 

Lying in his own blood, Elm looked up at his defender and softly confessed the truth: he was a police officer. Ash’s eyes hardened; he raised his pistol and shot Elm just as heavily armed tactical units stormed the warehouse, cutting Ash down in a hail of gunfire.

A gun discharges into a motel room wall, grazing flesh, and Aaron Vale tells Wes Tarrow to run. Elsewhere, in a quiet suburban kitchen, Lena Ward packs school lunches for her two young daughters and her husband, Doug, enjoying a settled, sober life far from her past addiction. 

In a stark hospital room, a doctor informs Aaron that his failing heart will kill him within weeks unless a donor is found. His estranged wife, Della, presses him to agree to be inseminated with his frozen sperm before he dies. 

In a different room, Lena demands that Wes be killed. Driven by her imperative, Aaron buys a revolver and tracks the man down. 

At a dimly lit crossing, a pickup truck strikes Doug and both young girls. The driver, Wes, hits the brakes, turns the vehicle back toward the scene, but panics and flees into the dark. At the hospital, a doctor informs Lena that her husband and both children are dead. Grief sends Lena back to cocaine, and she begins methodically destroying herself.

Aaron leaves Della, telling her he does not want the child she is trying to conceive. By then, he is unable to stop thinking about whose heart is beating in his chest. Doug’s heart was transplanted into Aaron, who woke up alive for the first time in months. Aaron hires a private investigator to find the donor’s widow, follows Lena, and engineers a meeting at a swimming pool. The two begin an affair. When he eventually admits to Lena that he is carrying her husband’s heart, she throws him out, then takes him back.

At a police station, Wes walks through the doors, confesses to the hit-and-run, and is sent back to prison. Previously, Wes was a newly born-again ex-convict holding down a job and coaching boys' baseball, even as his wife Nita dreaded his fanaticism and his temper. Upon being released early, Wes walks out on Nita and on his faith, taking work at a motel far from home.

Bleeding and shaken, Wes follows the pair back to their motel room and asks Aaron to finish the job. Instead of firing again, Aaron turns the gun on himself. Lena and Wes get the dying Aaron to a hospital where the transplanted heart fails. Afterward, Wes goes home to his family, while Lena, pregnant, goes home alone.

As an insurance investigator, Martin Kray once interviewed a claimant named Elias Prine, ruling his memory loss psychosomatic and denying the claim. Deprived of the payout, Elias’s diabetic wife tested her husband by asking for injection after injection, dying of an overdose he could not remember giving her. 

In a derelict basement, Martin beat and strangled the drug dealer Gil Marsh, photographing the corpse. As he died, Gil whispered the name "Elias," a mystery Martin could not explain as he changed into the dead man's suit and took his sports car.

Tragedy soon struck Martin directly when intruders attacked him and his wife in their bathroom. Though Martin killed one assailant, a blow to his head destroyed his ability to form new memories, forcing him to create a rigid system of instant photographs, annotated notes, and tattoos to hunt the second attacker, known only as R.M.

Roy arrived at the basement and revealed a devastating truth: Gil was innocent, Martin had already avenged his wife a year prior, and Martin was actually the man in the Prine story. Refusing to believe him, Martin burned the photos of Gil, scribbled "he is lying to you" on Roy’s picture, copied down the officer's license plate, and drove to a tattoo parlor to ink the numbers onto his thigh as his sixth permanent fact.

About a year before his current hunt, a plainclothes officer named Roy had helped Martin track down and slay the real attacker—a victory Martin forgot within minutes. Incapable of retaining his grief, Martin stood in an open field burning his wife's hairbrush and books, attempting to mourn a loss that continually dissolved from his mind.

At her bar, Gil’s girlfriend Corinne instantly recognized her dead lover’s clothes and car, serving Martin a beer her staff had spat in. Seeking revenge, Corinne hid every pen in her house, goaded Martin into striking her, and then used her fresh bruises to blame a man named Vance so Martin would hunt him down.

Sitting in a motel room he could not remember checking into, Martin held the telephone receiver, narrating the entire Prine case to an anonymous caller. The voice on the line fed Martin a name and a location, falsely identifying Gil Marsh as the killer he sought.

Driven by Corinne’s lie, Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, severely beat him, and drove him out of town at gunpoint. Returning victorious, Martin received a state vehicle record from Corinne, who had run the license plate through a contact; the paper named Roy Mercer. Luring Roy back to the derelict building where Gil had died, Martin shot the officer in the head and raised his camera to photograph the fresh corpse.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war delivered to a young boy the gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of captivity. Decades later, that boy was the ageing boxer Denny. Denny double-crossed his employer Otis, won his fight, and killed his opponent in the ring before escaping the arena in a taxi. Hiding in a motel with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovered she had left his father’s watch behind in his flat. Denny returned to the flat for the watch and shot the hitman Rollo dead with a submachine gun left resting on the kitchen counter. Fleeing the scene, Denny and Otis collided in the street, crashed, and were taken prisoner in the basement of a pawnshop. Denny broke free, coming back with a sword seized from the shop wall while one of their captors was raping Otis. Grateful for the rescue, Otis declared them square on the condition that Denny leave town forever. Denny collected Marielle and rode out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop.

Meanwhile, a mysterious briefcase defined a separate sequence of encounters. Hitmen Rollo and Marcus drove across the city debating foreign drug laws and what fast food is called abroad. Waiting in the corridor outside their target's flat, the two argued over whether a foot massage is worth killing a man for. Stepping inside, Marcus recited a passage of scripture and the pair shot a young man named Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis, and recovered the briefcase. Suddenly, a fourth man hidden in the bathroom emptied a revolver at them without hitting either, an outcome Marcus called divine intervention. In the car afterwards, Rollo's gun went off and blew the head off their passenger Del. Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren's house, where a sharp fixer directed the cleanup and gave the men fresh clothes. Over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner they were sitting in. Marcus talked the robber down mid-holdup, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase, and let the couple walk out. The two hitmen then delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar, where Otis was paying Denny to take a dive in the fifth.

Finally, the path of illicit substances brought its own ruin. Rollo bought heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up before his night out. Rollo took Otis's wife Nadia to a themed diner where they entered and won the dance contest. Later, Nadia snorted Rollo's heroin, overdosed, and was narrowly revived by an adrenaline shot to the heart on the dealer's living-room floor.

Nadir stood in the gun shop beside his daughter Sahar, swallowing his pride as the dealer openly mocked his foreign accent while handing over the handgun. Across town that same evening, Trey and Kwame ambushed the prosecutor Halstead outside a dimly lit restaurant, speeding off in his stolen car.

Later that night, Officer Voss would stand on a dark rural road, watching his patrol car consume Kwame’s dead body in a roar of orange flames. Voss had picked up the young hitchhiker, but when Kwame reached into his pocket, Voss misread the gesture, shot him dead, and torched the vehicle to erase the mistake.

Before that fatal encounter took place, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay Hobart and his wife Renee. Boyle groped Renee right in front of her helpless husband before letting them go with a smug warning. Disgusted, Boyle’s partner Voss went straight to their commander to demand a new patrol car rather than keep riding with a racist. 

Meanwhile, a locksmith named Mateo arrived at the Halstead home to change the locks. Paula Halstead watched him with hostility, loudly declaring he was a gang member who would sell her keys. Undeterred, Mateo moved on to Nadir’s shop. After fixing the latch, Mateo warned the shopkeeper that the frame itself was broken, but Nadir angrily accused him of running a con. 

Tragedy tightened its grip everywhere. Boyle pleaded desperate hours with a cold health insurance clerk named Delia Frank to approve treatment for his dying father, only to be refused. That night, Nadir’s shop was smashed and looted, and his insurer refused to pay a dime because he had ignored Mateo's warning about the door. 

Retribution took strange forms. When Renee Hobart was trapped upside down in a burning car wreck, it was Boyle—the officer who had violated her—who crawled through the flames and dragged her out. Not far away, Trey and Kwame struck a shopkeeper named Pham with their vehicle, panicking just enough to dump his bleeding body outside a hospital. 

When Clay Hobart tried to reclaim his stolen car, officers caught him mid-carjacking; Voss intervened just in time, talking the frantic cops out of shooting him. Clay then drove Trey away from the pursuing police at breakneck speed before shoving him out onto the pavement.

Consuming revenge drove Nadir to Mateo’s house. He waited outside in the shadows with his gun. As Mateo stepped into the yard and his small daughter Rosie ran eagerly into his arms, Nadir pulled the trigger. The gunshot cracked, but the child was completely untouched; Sahar had secretly bought blanks. Staring at the uninjured girl, Nadir wept, convinced she was his guardian angel.

It was after this that Kwame went hitchhiking on that lonely highway, where Voss shot him dead and burned the car. Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the scorched roadside where his brother’s body lay, only to face his grieving mother, who bitterly blamed Isaiah for never once going to look for Kwame.

The city spiraled further into isolation. Paula Halstead fell down her grand staircase and lay bruised on the floor, whispering to her housekeeper Alba that she was the only real friend she had left. Trey, wandering near the docks, discovered Pham’s abandoned van packed with terrified, trafficked migrants; instead of selling them, he unlocked the doors and turned them all free into the night.

Finally, as the first snow of the year began to fall, another violent collision rang out through the street, starting yet another furious argument in the cold.

Disgusted, Boyle’s partner Voss went straight to their commander to demand a new patrol car rather than keep riding with a racist. 

Meanwhile, a locksmith named Mateo arrived at the Halstead home to change the locks. Paula Halstead watched him with hostility, loudly declaring he was a gang member who would sell her keys. Undeterred, Mateo moved on to Nadir’s shop. After fixing the latch, Mateo warned the shopkeeper that the frame itself was broken, but Nadir angrily accused him of running a con. 

Tragedy tightened its grip everywhere. Boyle pleaded desperate hours with a cold health insurance clerk named Delia Frank to approve treatment for his dying father, only to be refused. That night, Nadir’s shop was smashed and looted, and his insurer refused to pay a dime because he had ignored Mateo's warning about the door. 

Retribution took strange forms. When Renee Hobart was trapped upside down in a burning car wreck, it was Boyle—the officer who had violated her—who crawled through the flames and dragged her out. Not far away, Trey and Kwame struck a shopkeeper named Pham with their vehicle, panicking just enough to dump his bleeding body outside a hospital. 

When Clay Hobart tried to reclaim his stolen car, officers caught him mid-carjacking; Voss intervened just in time, talking the frantic cops out of shooting him. Clay then drove Trey away from the pursuing police at breakneck speed before shoving him out onto the pavement.

Consuming revenge drove Nadir to Mateo’s house. He waited outside in the shadows with his gun. As Mateo stepped into the yard and his small daughter Rosie ran eagerly into his arms, Nadir pulled the trigger. The gunshot cracked, but the child was completely untouched; Sahar had secretly bought blanks. Staring at the uninjured girl, Nadir wept, convinced she was his guardian angel.

It was after this that Kwame went hitchhiking on that lonely highway, where Voss shot him dead and burned the car. Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the scorched roadside where his brother’s body lay, only to face his grieving mother, who bitterly blamed Isaiah for never once going to look for Kwame.

The city spiraled further into isolation. Paula Halstead fell down her grand staircase and lay bruised on the floor, whispering to her housekeeper Alba that she was the only real friend she had left. Trey, wandering near the docks, discovered Pham’s abandoned van packed with terrified, trafficked migrants; instead of selling them, he unlocked the doors and turned them all free into the night.

Finally, as the first snow of the year began to fall, another violent collision rang out through the street, starting yet another furious argument in the cold.

Ruben lived in a cramped house alongside his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor’s wife Alma, and their infant baby. Life at home was bitter: Nestor spent his nights robbing a pharmacy and his days beating Alma, driving Ruben to press her repeatedly to run away with him. Seeking an escape, Ruben discovered that Nestor’s vicious rottweiler, Tigre, killed any other dog on sight, so he began entering the animal into local dogfights and compiled a steady streak of victories. Trying to break Nestor's grip, Ruben paid two thugs to beat his brother. Nestor retaliated ruthlessly, snatching Alma, the baby, and Ruben’s hidden savings before vanishing completely. In Tigre's final fight, the promoter Chaco drew a gun and shot the dog right in the ring; Ruben instantly stabbed Chaco and fled the scene with his friend Pipo. Speeding recklessly through town to escape, Ruben ran a red light at full speed and ploughed into another car. Months later, after Nestor was shot dead while robbing a bank, Ruben attended the funeral and made one last offer to Alma to leave with him, but she refused.

Model Celine Vaz occupied a very different sphere. Her married lover Hector had walked out on his wife and daughters to move Celine into a stylish new flat that faced a towering billboard bearing her own glamorous image. That life disintegrated in an instant when Ruben’s runaway car slammed into hers. Celine woke up in a hospital bed with her shattered leg pinned together, frantic over her lapdog Chispa, who was lost somewhere inside the new flat. In reality, Chispa had fallen through a hole in the floorboards; Hector spent his days frantically tearing up the floor while, in the hospital, Celine’s pinned leg grew infected and turned gangrenous. Ultimately, Celine’s leg was amputated, and the billboard carrying her picture was taken down.

Cardo, a former guerrilla turned vagrant contract killer, was standing at the junction when the crash occurred and dragged the bleeding Tigre out of the smoking wreck. Cardo nursed the battered dog back to health among his own pack of strays. Driven by old ghosts, Cardo stood far off watching as his estranged wife was buried, afterward following his grown daughter Perla back to her home. Soon, the businessman Elian hired Cardo to murder his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Rather than killing him, Cardo abducted Sergio and chained him up in his hidden lair. He then brought Elian face to face with his brother, left a loaded pistol resting between them, and walked away having extracted money from both. Returning home, Cardo found that Tigre had slaughtered every other dog in his yard while he was out; Cardo pressed a gun to the rottweiler’s head, but could not bring himself to fire. Finally, Cardo broke into Perla’s flat, took her photograph, and recorded a long confession explaining who he was on her answering machine. Shaved and wearing clean clothes, Cardo left his money for Perla and walked out into the vast wasteland with Tigre.

Helicopters sprayed the city for crop pests through the night, passing low over every neighbourhood. In the quiet morning that followed, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, got ready for an upcoming dinner party. Across town at his shop, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake for a boy called Charlie Rill. 

Later that morning on his way to school, young Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by a waitress called Rhona, though he picked himself up and walked home insisting he was fine. Soon after reaching his front door, Charlie collapsed into a coma, leaving his parents Grant and Elaine to keep a desperate vigil at the hospital. While they watched over the boy, Grant's estranged father Duff turned up at the hospital bedside and unexpectedly confessed an affair from decades ago. Meanwhile, unpaid for the ordered cake and completely ignored by the distracted parents, the baker started making anonymous, menacing phone calls to the family's house.

Elsewhere in the city, telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu seethed silently beside her. Seeking an escape, Stu and three friends drove out to the river to fish, only to find a young woman's body floating face down in the water. Rather than reporting it immediately, the men tethered the body to the riverbank and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone. When word finally got out, Vern's wife Iris, who worked as a party clown, was thoroughly disgusted when she learned what the men had done.

Life carried on in distant corners of the municipality. The singer Vida performed nightly in a smoky club while her cellist daughter Bee played alone at home in the quiet house. Around the same time, Officer Rowe, who was cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, callously abandoned the family dog in the middle of nowhere just to cover one of his lies. Discovery came quickly elsewhere; Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and flew into a rage, sawing her furniture to pieces. 

Across town, Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans, passing the hours by taking grotesque photographs of Dot made up to look like a beaten corpse. Later that evening, at the long-planned dinner party, Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an old affair, causing Neil to fly temperamental and make a furious public scene. 

In the sterile light of the intensive care unit, young Charlie died in the hospital. Driven by grief and anger over the harassment, Grant and Elaine went straight to the bakery to confront Otto; instead of fighting, the old baker fed them warm bread and grieved openly with them. 

Tragedy rippled further into the night. Finding her mother asleep after her show, Bee closed the garage door and killed herself with the car engine running. Out in the shadows at a picnic in the hills, Stu lost control and smashed a young woman's head with a heavy rock. 

Finally, a violent tremor shook the entire city, and every death and every wreck was folded into one single, devastating evening news bulletin.

Dressed as devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew robbed a diamond house in a northern port, walking out with a huge stone. Overseas, his cousin Marv got word of the heist and told Solly to bring the diamond straight over to him. Before Solly departed, Grigor the Nail told him about a bookmaker’s in the city, but simultaneously tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob Solly at that very shop. 

Meanwhile, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. The deal went sour when a bare-knuckle fighter named Finn knocked Sam out cold, leaving Halloway without a fighter for the gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout. Desperate, Halloway was forced to put Finn into the fight instead, promising Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city, delivered the diamond to a fence named Hersch, and headed straight for the bookmaker’s to place his bet on the fight. At the shop, Ike, Benno, and their accomplice Tulley bungled the robbery; they severed Solly’s arm and grabbed his handcuffs-bound case, only to be chased off by Grigor. Later at the ring, Finn ignored his instructions and knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a vast fortune on the outcome and brutally took his fury out on Halloway.

Having heard nothing from his cousin, Marv flew in, found Solly missing, and hired the ruthless bounty hunter Ledge to locate him. Grigor, meanwhile, captured the crippled Solly and cut off his remaining arm to open the case, only to discover the diamond was not inside. Ledge quickly traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took both the pawnbrokers and the stone they had managed to procure. Coldstone took Solly from Grigor's web and fed him alive to his pigs, before warning Halloway and Digby in graphic detail what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby immediately instructed Finn to go down in the fourth round of the rematch. To ensure compliance, Coldstone’s men set fire to a caravan, burning Finn’s mother to death inside. 

While the tension mounted before the bout, Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car with Ike and Benno trapped inside. In the violent shootout that followed, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Amidst the carnage, Tulley slipped away into the night, accompanied only by a stray dog that had swallowed the diamond during the chaos.

When the night of the rematch arrived, Finn fought fiercely until the fourth round, but instead of taking a dive, he knocked his opponent out cold again. Simultaneously, the vengeful travellers who had quietly infiltrated the arena massacres Coldstone’s men in the crowd. Taking advantage of the uproar, Halloway and Digby tracked Coldstone down to his office and shot him dead. By morning, the camp of travellers had completely vanished without a trace.

Days later, the stray dog was handed in at a local pet shop. While in its cage, the animal coughed up the diamond, and through a twist of fate, Halloway and Digby ended up holding the precious stone at last.

High above the dark city street, in a quiet flat overlooking the asphalt, an old man stood speaking to a younger one, explaining softly that nothing ultimately survives time. Outside the window below them, flashing emergency lights cut through the night as police officers handcuffed Cort and Jonah, forcibly carrying the pair out of the club’s entrance and into the cold air.

In the chaotic interior of the Pit moments earlier, violence had erupted. Jonah had grabbed a heavy fire extinguisher and beaten a man’s face into a bloody ruin, entirely unaware that the real Adder was standing merely a few feet away, watching the fatal mistake with cold eyes. Cort had initiated the commotion by hunting relentlessly through the crowded venue, recklessly seizing the wrong man, who had twisted Cort's arm until the bone violently snapped.

Before storming the club, Cort and Jonah had been approached in the street by two shadowy men who offered to sell them the rapist’s name, directing the vengeful pair toward the dark doorway of the Pit. Cort and Jonah had steeled themselves after stepping outside the party into the night, only to find Lise already surrounded by paramedics and being loaded into the back of an ambulance.

Underneath the city, the assault had been terrible. In the pedestrian underpass, the Adder had brutally raped Lise, slamming her head repeatedly against the hard concrete. A solitary passer-by had caught a brief glimpse of the horror in the dim light, but terrified, had backed away and fled into the night. Lise had taken the stairs down into the passage simply to avoid crossing a busy road, walking unsuspectingly into the shadows where the Adder was already in the middle of beating a transsexual woman.

She had been wandering the streets alone because she had walked out on the party in absolute disgust. Inside the crowded apartment, Cort had gotten steadily drunk and high, shameless as he openly pursued other women across the room. Just hours before that betrayal, Lise, Cort, and Jonah had ridden the underground train together to get to the gathering, their voices rising in cheerful arguments about sex and Cort’s heavy drinking.

Before that ill-fated night, Lise had spent an afternoon sitting in a bright park. Children played in the grass around her, running among the spray of sprinklers, while she read a book with one hand resting protectively over her stomach. She was still processing the quiet shock from earlier, when, entirely alone in her flat, she had taken a pregnancy test and watched the indicator reveal a positive result.

Long before the child, the party, or the nightmare beneath the street, there had been only a quiet morning in bed. Lise lay beside Cort, warm beneath the covers, describing a recurring dream she kept having about a red tunnel. Cort had laughed, pulling her close, as the two of them teased each other playfully about her ex-boyfriend, Jonah.

In the dim evening light of the townhouse, Emlyn looked at his oldest friend and spoke with quiet finality. He had known about the affair for four full years, he admitted, ever since his wife had told him during their journey abroad; besides, he added coldly, he had never thought much of Wilder’s letters anyway.

Earlier that same evening, Wilder had dialed Emlyn’s number in a frantic state. Panicked and undone by what he had just learned, he begged to see him, and Emlyn agreed to come to his house without hesitation.

The agitation had begun hours before in the quiet booth of a local bar. As they sat over drinks, Odile had casually let slip a piece of infuriating news: Emlyn had recently agreed to publish a particular author—a writer represented by Wilder whom both men quietly detested.

It was during that same conversation in the bar that Odile delivered her first shock, revealing that her marriage was officially over. She explained to Wilder that she had spent the previous night confessing every detail of her long betrayal to her husband.

Two years prior to that afternoon in the bar, their secret domesticity had come to an unsentimental end. Deciding between them that the rented rooms had turned into nothing more than a tedious chore, Wilder and Odile methodically divided their accumulated crockery and surrendered the lease.

Before the apartment was abandoned, there had been an evening when Wilder sat as a guest at the married couple's dinner table. Throughout the meal, Emlyn and Wilder engaged in endless, deliberate talk of racquet games and old schoolboy sports, driving the conversation until Odile had no part in the talk at all.

Days before that dinner, Emlyn had taken Wilder out for a long, heavy lunch at a city restaurant. Drinking straight through the meal, Emlyn spent the hours baiting the book agent about the state of contemporary fiction, never once dropping his guard or mentioning the bitter truth he had learned.

Yet when Odile returned to the secret apartment shortly after her trip, she said nothing whatever about what had transpired abroad. She met Wilder in silence, and the afternoon passed exactly as the others had.

The silence had been broken days earlier in a hotel room abroad. There, Odile had finally confessed the truth, only for Emlyn to remark that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Her confession had been provoked moments prior, when Emlyn questioned her in the hotel. He asked about a letter held for her at the desk, addressed in a handwriting he recognized all too well.

Months before the trip abroad, Odile had stood in their rented flat and broken momentous news to her lover. She announced that she was carrying her husband’s child, but after a brief pause, the pair decided the rented rooms would go on exactly as before.

They had established those rooms in a quiet district months earlier, eager to give their secret life a tangible reality. Together, they had filled them with linen and plates, giving the affair a household of its own.

Long before the flat existed, there had been a party at the house of Emlyn’s closest friend. While the other guests drank downstairs, Wilder had led Odile to an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was.

Long before the flat existed, there had been a party at the house of Emlyn’s closest friend. While the other guests drank downstairs, Wilder had led Odile to an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was.

A beam weapon flashes, bright and absolute, cutting through his neck just after he finishes addressing the gathered crowd. He falls silently to the pavement, having known the precise shape and outcome of this public execution all along. Far across the stars, inside a transparent display enclosure on a distant planet, a famous film actress shares a plush couch with him while green, plunger-like extraterrestrials explain that every single moment in time exists simultaneously across eternity, and that free will is merely a foolish, ignorant concept unique to his home world. His daughter sits at a polished desk, signing legal affidavits to take full control of his financial affairs, convinced that her father has become hopelessly senile.

He lies motionless upon the blue tiles at the bottom of a deep pool, watching the watery light ripple above him after his father hurls him into the deep end to force him to learn to swim. In a dreary, soot-stained industrial town, an infant is born weak and peculiar, marked from his very first breath as a frail oddity. On a late-night radio broadcast, he leans close to the studio microphone, attempting patiently to explain the fourth dimension, the nature of time, and his experiences in the alien enclosure to an incredulous host.

High in a frozen mountain range, he stumbles away from the burning, twisted debris of a crashed airliner as its sole unharmed survivor, completely unaware that his wife is perishing at that exact hour from lethal carbon monoxide exhaust fumes trapped inside her vehicle while driving frantically toward the emergency room. He marries the daughter of a prominent man who owns an optometry school, an advantageous union that elevates him into immense wealth. Following a sudden physical collapse upon his return home, he reposes in a hospital bed where a neighboring patient introduces him to the obscure, poorly written novels of a local hack science fiction writer.

A fellow captive whispers through the darkness of the barracks, swearing a solemn oath to hire an assassin who will murder him one day on account of the dead scout. Lost behind enemy lines in a bitter winter, a hardened scout beats him repeatedly across the face for slumping into the snow and begging to be left alone to die. The captured pair are locked into a foul cattle car, where the scout’s wounded leg slowly rots with gangrene until he dies on the wooden floor, cursing the chaplain’s assistant with his last breath. In a quiet prison camp, he spends his days beside enemy officers who have comfortably drawn double rations for several years, sustained entirely by an uncorrected clerical error in the quartermaster’s ledger. He was pressed into service as a chaplain’s assistant, shipped across the ocean with no military training worth the name.

An immense firestorm destroys a magnificent city in a single night, incinerating millions of structures while he and a group of prisoners remain unharmed inside an underground meat locker. When they finally open the heavy doors and climb to the surface, they find the entire metropolis erased.
